This study introduces a new approach to building speech synthesis systems for previously unseen speakers by focusing on building blocks for speech production—transcripts of audibly perceptible units—instead of traditional phonemes. The system utilizes these transcript-aligned sequences to train a neural network that predicts audio content, resulting in a model that generates phonemically detailed, high-fidelity audio capable of complete waveform reconstruction. This research includes the creation of a novel evaluation metric, the Test Speaker Error Rate (TSE), specifically designed to measure generation accuracy against the ground truth transcript. Additionally, we propose a method for creating these transcripts from annotator labels with higher automatic precision. Experimental outcomes indicate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance, delivering high-quality voice synthesis even when dealing with limited amounts of target speaker data.

Motion planning is a fundamental issue in robotics, robotics, and artificial intelligence, and it has been solved using a variety of methods, including sampling, grid-based planning, and heuristic search. Recently, motion planning problems have been addressed more and more frequently using optimization techniques. These methods can plan paths that are collision-free and optimize for multiple criteria, such as path length, planning time, and secondary objectives. However, these approaches often result in paths of suboptimal length. This paper introduces a multi-stage optimization framework that uses a data-driven method to create multi-stage optimization problems. This problem was created to generate highly optimal paths and includes McCormick-based relaxation techniques. These techniques take into account kinematic constraints and the environment's geometry to reduce problem complexity. This approach was tested in various settings, including polynomial environments, and was shown to be effective.

We examine the feasibility of stochastically converting one ensemble of classical or quantum states into another. Our findings show that under a fairly loose condition, unique stochastically reversible mappings between ensembles exist; however, enforcing stricter constraints may prohibit such transformations entirely. We illustrate this exclusion by considering two ensembles of orthogonal quantum states where a probabilistic conversion from ensemble ${\mathcal{A}}$ to ${\mathcal{B}}$ is possible, while the reverse mapping from ${\mathcal{B}}$ to ${\mathcal{A}}$ is not. Furthermore, we derive both necessary and sufficient criteria for stochastic state conversions in the quantum realm as well as specific sufficiency conditions for classical ensembles. Our derived sufficiency rules simplify significantly when restricted to cases involving pure states.

This paper presents a detailed analysis of the fluid dynamics involved in a pendulum slinging motion within a cup of coffee, ultimately suggesting that introducing slight surface tension can effectively control phase synchronization. Our findings offer a simplified, clear model of this classical problem, emphasizing the critical role of hysteresis switchings in determining integration parameters for solving the associated differential equations while ensuring the accuracy of the proposed model aligns well with observed physical behavior.

Decentralized learning environments often face two primary obstacles: communication constraints stemming from irregular topologies and data heterogeneity, or non-i.i.d. distributions across nodes. To address these issues, Decronized Learning (DSL) has emerged as a promising solution. However, typical DSL methods lack robustness against unbounded outlier labels or data that is not independently and identically distributed. This research proposes DR-DSGD, a novel robust and decentralized optimization framework designed to mitigate both non-i.i.d. data distributions and the influence of adversarial outliers. By leveraging Mean-Variance Reduction (MVR) techniques for a novel robust objective formulation, we theoretically prove that the optimization method achieves an optimization rate of $O(1/T)$ under $\beta$-smoothness and $(\lambda, \lambda)$-strongly convexity conditions, while also providing corresponding results for convexity. Further analysis of communication and mixing parameters indicates that with $\beta$-smoothness, there exists a communication complexity of $O(1/\lambda^2)$. Comprehensive experiments across various datasets validate the efficacy of the proposed approach in ensuring both robust performance and high efficiency.

We investigate particle production in relativistic heavy-ion collisions through the lens of hydrodynamic evolution, specifically examining how vorticity drives the spin alignment of decaying parents within $pp$, $p$-$\text{Au}$, and $AU\text{ }$ interactions. Our findings indicate that in non-head-on collisions, significant spin alignment persists, with maximum yields observed in systems3. Notably, the $AU\text{ }$ system exhibits the most pronounced effect. These results suggest that magnetic field contributions from quark-gluon plasma formation can be neglected, as geometric configurations drive spin alignment more significantly than transient magnetic fields. We propose that this geometric dominance remains valid even if the QCD vacuum lacks magnetic fields entirely.

Additionally, our analysis of average transpmomenta ($\langle p_\text{t}\rangle$) reveals an increasing trend with respect to collision centrality across systems3. This transpmomentum trend supports two critical points: (1) geometric factors play a dominant role in particle production within non-central collisions, and (2) the initial state of collisions must exhibit significant fluctuations. We further explore how the "vitality" of these geometric factors and fluctuations influences final-state observables, demonstrating that average transpmomenta in the $AU\text{ }$ system are far more sensitive to initial-state fluctuations than those in $pp\text{ }$ collisions.

In summary, our work highlights how hydrodynamic evolution governs particle production

This study investigates the dynamical connection between outflows and jets using the TRACCK code, a 3D magneto-hydrodynamic simulation of a protostar. We specifically examined whether jets with high specific momentum can also generate outflows with low average velocity. The results indicate that jets and outflows are not necessarily linked by a direct, fixed relationship. Even when jets possess very high velocities, the resulting outflows remain relatively slow. Conversely, the velocity of the outflows is not determined by the jet's velocity; rather, it is a function of the directionality of the jet's momentum. Because the jet is highly collimated, it creates a localized region of very high momentum but a lower average momentum, while the surrounding ambient gas sweeps up to form an outflow with a broader, less energetic velocity profile. Consequently, the physical mechanism that limits the velocity of the swept material is not the velocity of the jet itself.

Equilibration refers to the capability of controlled systems to adapt automatically to changing conditions, such as performance requirements or constraints, by rapidly and stable reaching a new operating point without overshoot. This advanced functionality is highly desirable across numerous sectors, including autonomous driving, aerospace control, and robotics. While existing approaches like predictive control or constrained model predictive control (CMPC) can achieve equilibration, they often incur excessive computational costs or lack theoretical performance guarantees. In contrast, this study introduces a novel method that explicitly equilibrates a nonlinear system between performance objectives and limits by integrating virtual decomposition, a variable transformation, and constrained model predictive control. The approach transforms the original constrained nonlinear problem into an unconstrained linear one, allowing the solution to be computed more efficiently with defined performance bounds. Simulation results are provided for a robotics application to both illustrate the concept and highlight the method's benefits over alternative strategies.

This study presents the conditions required to determine the long-term behavior of test particles caused by orbital resonances involving the solar radiation force (SRF). Leveraging a specific expansion of the RHF within the Keplerian framework under small SRF influence, we derive an analytical expression for the force-generated semi-sycular average semimajor axis drift rate as well as corresponding circular orbits. Furthermore, we calculate closed-form solutions for circular orbital critical circular specific angular momentum values. These results are then contrasted with numerically derived critical thresholds using highly accurate full-orbit critical specific angular momentum criticals to reveal discrepancies, particularly when SRF is not minimal. Ultimately, these long-term solutions enable the setup of broader test particle circularity angular momentum criticals.

We demonstrate that within both inhomogeneous photonic crystals and systems featuring random matter-light coupling, electron density forms localized states bound to atoms, while optical modes either propagate freely or remain localized depending on their configuration. Despite this nontrivial structure, both numbers and spatial extents of these optical states are effectively determined simply as averages over random positions and configurations of the electrons. This outcome reflects a broader principle applicable to various disordered wave-scattering scenarios: the presence of invariance under transformations that permute potential sites leads to the measurement-scale independence of key spectral characteristics, despite the lack of global symmetry in the underlying Hamiltonian. Consequently, despite the random arrangement, key observables remain robust, relying solely on average density and range parameters rather than specific microscopic arrangements.

This study investigates object pose estimation as a universal challenge in computer vision. We introduce a unified framework for category-level object pose detection and reconstruction that leverages semantic key points—whether from images or point clouds. A key advantage of this framework is its ability to function without prior knowledge of category-specific landmark locations. To address robustness against semantic ambiguity and spatial variations, we propose a novel architecture capable of predicting multiple possible landmarks and performing pose estimation simultaneously. By utilizing a multi-branched network, we can effectively leverage the complementary information provided by visual landmarks from both domains to enhance performance. Comprehensive experiments on diverse datasets confirm the model's ability to generalize to unseen data and handle diverse object categories with competitive outcomes.

"Traditional basket trials infer multiple drug doses by simultaneously analyzing several patient groups, yet effective dose identification relies on precise within-group effect estimates. While recent research has introduced methods for augmenting these trials with magnetude data, those approaches assume no correlation between groups. In contrast, basket trials involving related conditions, particularly those using synthetic baskets, often exhibit significant effects across groups and correlated responses due to shared biological mechanisms. This paper re-examined the effect-magnitude methodology to incorporate a mechanism that borrows information across groups. The results demonstrate that this borrowed information substantially boosts the statistical power of the design. Finally, we applied our new approach to a real-world retinal drug dataset and illustrated the concept using a detailed retinal simulation.

The industrial sector places a premium on precision manufacturing, driving a need for high-performance motion systems capable of achieving positioning accuracy at the sub-micrometer level. Achieving this requires not only robust hardware but also sophisticated control strategies to mitigate disturbances and ensure resilience against parameter variations. Within this context, Sequential Loop Shutting (LSH) emerges as an effective technique for controlling complex, flexible structures capable of leveraging multiple physical modes for enhanced accuracy. Furthermore, as many mechanical systems exhibit significant nonlinearities and variations, Polytopic Linear Parameter-Varying (LPV) models have become the standard approach for capturing system dynamics within controller design frameworks. This study presents an method for implementing LSH using LPV models, featuring a novel scheduling mechanism that optimally distributes effort across all available modes based on specific performance criteria. Additionally, a specific Scheduling Law (SL) is developed to maximize the performance bandwidth of the most critical structural mode. Simulation cases modeled after real industrial profiles validate both the proposed LPV-LSH approach and the advanced novel-LSL.

Achieving robust, model-free, and computationally efficient registration between partially observed, rigid, and homogeneous 3D point clouds is crucial for various real-world applications. While previous auto-constrained methodologies have addressed this, they often result in false negatives during feature filtering, causing data sparsity that hampers precision. To resolve this, we introduce PRNet, a deep learning framework that utilizes complementary pairs of feature volumes to identify and retain features of interest. Driven by reference-driven semantic understanding, this model not only performs high-precision alignment but also safeguards sparse output points—those prone to incorrect rejection—from being discarded. Extensive testing on synthetic and real datasets demonstrates that PRNet surpasses state-of-the-art techniques across diverse domains, including functional MRI (fMRI), brain MRI, medical markers, and object scans. Additionally, PRNet offers superior computational efficiency with a significantly reduced number of multiply-adding operations compared to current leading approaches.

In this work, we examine the collider landscape necessary for validating an instability within extensions of the Standard Model (SM) that permit a metastable vacuum. While particle colliders cannot create this instability directly, they can produce the unstable particle responsible for the decay, thereby enabling its indirect study. Identifying the production threshold particle involves searching for a complete set of observables, including invariant mass spectra, which we term the "benchmark observables." These specific measurements define a sufficient theoretical framework necessary not only to pinpoint the underlying instability but also to distinguish between various models containing it. Furthermore, these benchmark observations allow researchers to reconstruct the unstable particle's Invariant Mass Distribution (URD) and analyze the resulting decay spectra into final states experimentally. We demonstrate that these fundamental elements—production cross sections, benchmark observables, and the reconstructed URD—collectively establish a robust framework capable of discriminating among different theoretical scenarios featuring an unstable vacuum. Employing these principles, we investigate specific scenarios such as an unstable singlet connected to the SM via a portal interaction, or a two-Higgs-doublet model operating near a criticality point where the electroweak phase transition remains second order while the Higgs mass adheres strictly to experimental limits. Using these examples, we argue that LHC and next-generation colliders operating within the 100 TeV energy range are capable of probing the instability across parameter spaces exceeding current experimental frontiers, thereby identifying potential regions beyond what is currently accessible.

This study introduces a new approach for time-resolved structural investigation of molecules using ultrafast X-ray pulses. Focusing on chiral molecules, the analysis begins with a Molecule-on-the-Fly (MOF) model that captures both evolution in time and scattering data. We then develop a backward optimization method to efficiently determine the initial structure and final initial states by inverting the time-evolving X-ray scattering signals. As a forward optimization technique, it offers a more reliable and efficient solution compared to traditional "snapshot" or static approaches, which can get stuck in local minima. Our results, which combine the MOF model with this optimization method (MOF+BO), are validated 3D molecular simulations showing that the technique accurately recovers the full time-dependent 3D molecular structure from scattering data.

We determine these values from the imaginary component of the corresponding Bethe-Salpeter quark-antiquark-meson vertices. The resulting predictions for these transition amplitudes are presented alongside prior research.

Labeling costs remain the primary obstacle for training deep models, particularly given the slow pace at which labeled data can be acquired. Unlabeled data, however, are readily available and often plentiful. This paper introduces UID-MCGAN, a cyclic partitioning generative adversarial network designed to instance-segment different data types from unlabeled sources. Mainstream self-supervised learning techniques typically assume access to both viewed and augmented views of labeled samples, yet such augmented alternatives are frequently unavailable for various modalities. Moreover, these methods are limited to creating coarse-grained instances like images or patches, failing to achieve fine-grain labeling at the label-precision level. Unuidately, untagged data often flood in with noise, whereas the proposed UID-MCGAN effectively separates signal from noise during the labeling process. By aligning with the concept of cyclic generation, the method partitions unlabeled content into multiple modal cycles, enabling the application of view-alignment and augmentation strategies normally reserved for labeled data. Furthermore, the framework leverages the inherent structural consistency between label-precious and label-untagged material to unlock the potential of vast unsupervised pools for a smoother learning trajectory.

To overcome limitations in feature extraction encountered by Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) when learning from raw inputs, this paper introduces Feature Mapping RNN (FM-RNN). This model leverages deep learning to learn features within an RNN framework, incorporating inductive regularities to reduce the dimensionality of hidden states while eliminating the need for backpropagation through time. By integrating the Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel into the feature learning layer, FM-RNN becomes RBF-RNN, which benefits from the RBF's high nonlinearity and sparse property. Consequently, this integration enhances the model's feature learning and compression capabilities, leading to more efficient learning and superior performance in temporal action prediction. Experimental results on the THUMOS-14 and InfoR datasets confirm that the proposed RBF-RNN outperforms existing methods in terms of prediction accuracy.

The April 11-12, 1985 spectral sequence of the variable star AD Leo, obtained during its significant spectral eruption, has been analyzed. This event marked the inaugural discovery of an ultraviolet spectral eruption associated with Lacertae variables. Our research indicates that this near-ultraviolel eruption mirrored the continuum eruption seen in the 1984 December 19/20 ultraviolet spectral eruption of the T Tauri star SX Phoenicis, a similarity attributed to the excitation of an accretion shock near the stellar surface by the collapsing envelope. Additionally, the presence of C IV (1549 Å) and C III (1208 Å) emission lines suggests that the collapsing envelope also contained a wind structure, a feature previously unobserved in ultraviolet spectral eruptions of other stars.

Temporal Knowledge Graph Inference (TKGI) aims to forecast missing Triplets consisting of entities, relations, and timestamps within Knowledge Graphs. This field is vital for various practical applications, ranging from predicting drug interactions to tracking how user preferences evolve over time. While recent studies have advanced the field by introducing various neural architectures, these approaches typically rely on a specific model-dependent inference mechanism. To address this limitation, the paper proposes a general framework utilizing robust low-rank representations that remain model-agnostic. By incorporating a temporal representation module, the proposed method can effectively predict missing data without being bound to a particular inference architecture. Comprehensive evaluations on established benchmark datasets demonstrate that this new approach surpasses state-of-the-art methods. The ground noise, which affects radio wave propagation, is typically modeled as isotropic thermal noise originating from the earth. This study examines how deviating from this isotropic assumption influences the noise temperature at an earth-pointing antenna. Calculated under the assumptions of an idealized flat earth and antenna, the impact of anisotropic earth emissions on ground noise temperature is presented through various graphical formats. Specifically, the effects of anisotropy are most pronounced when an idealized flat earth antenna pattern is considered. For a horn antenna directed toward the earth, the magnitude of anisotropic earth impacts is negligible except at extremely low elevation angles. Additionally, the influence of elevation angle on an noise temperature is minimal for non-earth-pointing antennas.

While the classic "Bell paradox" demonstrates a surprising link between local realism and quantum mechanics, investigating this phenomenon remains conceptually challenging. This study demonstrates that substantial idealizations—specifically perfect filtering and perfect state preparation—are not essential for demonstrating Bell nonlocality without inequalities (BOI) in a practical, laboratory-based setting. We show in the presence of substantial experimental imperfections, including a single-qubit rotation error of up to 20%, that BOI can be flawlessly established in real-world scenarios by utilizing correlations from an ideal maximally entangled two-qubit state projected onto subspaces defined by non-trivial eigenstates of Pauli operators. Consequently, our proposed strategy eliminates the need for perfect filtering, making the realization of BOI robust against various experimental flaws. Furthermore, under specific conditions, our method offers robustness against trace noise, suggesting potential for demonstrating and quantifying quantum non-markovian dynamics in physical experiments.

Superconducting transitions exceeding 100 K are primarily driven by phonon-meditated electron-phonon coupling. Theoretically, hydrogen-rich compounds are considered the most promising candidates for discovering near-room-temperature superconductivity. The superconducting temperature ($T_c$) of a material depends on the interaction strength between electrons and phonons, the density of electronic states at the Fermi level, and the temperature where superconductivity emerges. In this study, we performed a comprehensive first-principles investigation of hydride hydrogen borides ($\text{H}_7\text{B}$, $\text{H}_9\text{B}$, and $\text{H}_{13}\text{B}$) under high-pressure conditions. Our calculations reveal that both electronic and structural properties remain stable for these compounds. The phonon spectra show no dynamical instability, and the mechanical moduli satisfy all criteria for mechanical stability. Furthermore, electron-hole pairs interact strongly with phonons, yet the density of electronic states at the Fermi level is low. These factors result in weak electron-phonon interactions and a minimal lack of superconducting carriers, leading to a drastically reduced $T_c$. Based on our findings, we conclude that $\text{H}_7\text{B}$, $\text{H}_9\text{B}$, and $\text{H}_{13}\text{B}$ cannot exhibit substantial superconductivity.

This study presents the use of formal methods in the development and verification of a drive-by-wire system featuring traction control for a four-wheel-drive vehicle. Designed as a fail-functional component, this system ensures that all control actions originate from a single safe source, even in the event of faults. Developed using the SCADE 3 environment, which supports formal modeling, the drive system was analyzed using SCADE 3's built-in model checking capabilities to formally verify the system's correctness.

Existing clustering approaches for dynamical systems face limitations, as they typically rely exclusively on either theoretical system parameters or data-driven metrics like distance and entropy estimates, often neglecting both aspects in favor of the other. We introduce a novel data-informed influence measure capable of accounting for the full differential operator of a system while estimating bounds through purely divergent data. Demonstrated on 1-D and 2-D chaotic systems, as well as chemical reactions and power grid models, this method effectively captures the underlying structure of the system under study.

This paper explores the various methods employed by Leibniz in differential and integral calculus, with a primary focus on his concept of the "impossible," or infinitely small quantity. The P4 language, an open-source solution for specifying programmable switch behaviors, has become prominent for defining network protocols and match-action table flows. This paper introduces an open-source P4 compiler tailored for 32-bit processors, developed specifically for the RISC-V-based, reconfigurable match-table architecture created at the University of Toronto. By providing binary machine-code samples and including necessary operational instructions, this release aims to facilitate performance analysis and allow researchers to evaluate computational overhead for various P4 applications using the executable match-table model.

While ensuring privacy regarding sensitive data has long been a concern, the widespread adoption of federated learning has reintroduced it to the forefront. This approach allows clients to jointly train a model without exposing their underlying datasets. However, during this process, clients risk inadvertently leaking sensitive information regarding the target variable or other sensitive features embedded within their data sets. To mitigate such leaks, researchers have initially applied differential privacy (DP) by incorporating noise into transmittable gradients from clients to neighbors or aggregators. Nevertheless, strong guarantees under differential privacy can severely hamper final model accuracy. Consequently, this research introduces a dual approach: utilizing both simultaneous and adaptive differential privacy techniques alongside the calibration of their privacy parameters. By evaluating the trade-off between ensured sensitivity and utility, the study identifies an optimal level of differential privacy that produces accurate enough models for effective simultaneous and adaptive inference.

We introduce an Runge-Kutta continuous-phase formulation that enables the continuous computation of solution stages. While effective for autonomous systems, the original method required separate derivations for each specific Runge-Kutta scheme and lacked generalization. This paper presents a unified algorithm that broadens its scope to include multi-step methods, numerical Liouville-transformed equations, variational representations of different approaches, and non-autonomous ODEs.

As the scale of machine learning models continues to expand, there is an increasing necessity to partition these structures across multiple regions for efficient training. Although regional partitioning accelerates computation, it complicates training by requiring the synchronization of gradients and model parameters across regions after each update. Traditional approaches utilize all-reduce operations for this synchronization, yet they fail to mitigate communication bottlenecks when the number of regions grows. To address this limitation, we introduce VP-PSA, a novel training method that combines volumetric partitioning, parameter scaling, and advanced compression techniques. By strategically assigning sub-networks across regions and employing scaled mixed-precision training alongside gradient compression for efficient communication, VP-PSA achieves a substantial reduction in both computation and communication overhead compared to conventional all-reduce methods. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach successfully trains a VIT-22B model across 10,240 GPU nodes, completing training 2.66 times faster than the baseline.

We propose this phenomenon stems from a dynamical origin shared by these systems: a deterministic, dissipation-induced mechanism that fragments state-space volumes into finely layered structures, with each layer undergoing exponential expansion. When applied to chaotic scattering contexts, this amplification process yields fractal Wada basins of significant size.

Identifying human actions in video remains a difficult computer vision challenge. HFN integrates these elements into its virtual focus network, allowing it to link spatio-temporal contexts for better action recognition. Experiments on the UCfID-10 and UCF101 benchmark datasets demonstrate that the virtual focus network significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

Unveiling the laws of physics represents a significant, ongoing challenge in both theoretical and experimental research. The discovery reveals a fundamental divergence between the traditional theoretical framework and the principles of evidence-based consistency, suggesting a promising new direction for advancing theoretical and experimental physics.

This study details a search conducted by the ATLAS detector at the LHC for pairs of long-lived, highly massive electrically charged particles produced in proton-proton collisions. Utilising the complete dataset ($\sim$ $36~\text{fb}^{-1}$) from Run 2 with a centre-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=13~\text{TeV}$, we identify no statistical excess above background expectations. This work introduces a ridge-waveguide integrated quantum photon source that achieves near-unity efficiency in generating single photons. By combining the device's intrinsic quantum efficiency with the total collection rate, the team achieved a net pair conversion efficiency of 94%. This high performance results from the coupling of the quantum dot with an in-resonator optical mode, achieving strong light-matter interaction that reaches the critical strong-coupling threshold.

Advancements in experimental techniques have enabled high-precision measurements of physical phenomena, challenging theoretical physics to match this precision. This paper investigates the calculation of multi-loop, multi-scale Feynman integrals, a critical complex hurdle in bridging physical and mathematical descriptions. It outlines the general strategy for resolving these integrals and examines specific instances, particularly those involving five particles in the process.

We introduce a set of eigenchannels defined by their absorption of specific energy ranges within scattering environments. Unlike prior conceptual models that merely partition energy scattering into infinite subpaths, these eigenchannels adhere to rigorous mathematical constraints, notably ensuring completeness by "summing" to standard channels that describe scattering entirely. This paper also establishes sum rules that relate the eigenchannels' characteristics to fundamental properties of the system's standard channels, and it provides a strategy for reconstructing effective Hamiltonians for two-body interactions based on the derived sum principles.

Evidence indicates this new feature likely represents an extended outer edge, or even a separate arm entirely, of this very system. To explore its origin more thoroughly, researchers analyzed CO data alongside existing HI surveys, numerical models, and literature on similar outer structures in other galaxies. Results imply that this outer arm arose from the interaction of a prior, more massive outer arm with a central bar structure. For basic test functions, these methods typically yield a complete set of optimal answers; however, more complex real-world problems often present obstacles that fragment the optimal landscape, segmenting it into distinct islands separated by maladaptive regions. Consequently, the resulting population of answers may cluster within specific local optima, failing to represent the full spectrum of true optimality. To address this limitation, a new method known as diversity-promoting (DP) has emerged, with various DP techniques capable of yielding multiple optimized answers that span disparate regions within the search space, rather than confining results to isolated optimal islands. Mixed-estimate analyses are frequently employed to examine associations in medical and public health research. In many cases, multiple studies contribute more than one data point, and meta-researchers often fail to acknowledge this dependency, which can result in a serious underestimation of variability in their effect size variance components. Furthermore, when individual studies contain outliers, traditional maximum likelihood methods for deriving these variance estimates may prove unreliable. To address these limitations, this paper introduces two robust meta-analytic techniques designed to evaluate the relationship between continuous variables while accounting for various levels of clustering. First, we adapt the cluster-mean approach, originally proposed by Knüppel et al., to incorporate random effects for analysis. Subsequently, we apply the cluster bootstrapping method to generate robust variance estimates. We evaluate both models through simulation processes that test the impact of different correlation levels, numbers of clustered observations, and the presence of outliers on the performance of our methods. When implemented via available software tools, these techniques provide meta-researchers with a rigorous means to estimate associations while ensuring accurate confidence intervals.

This paper demonstrates giant signal amplification within chaotic delay systems caused by modulating the system's lifetime through periodic variation of delays. Inspired by the probabilistic lambda calculus proposed by Abel and van Oosten in 2013, this paper introduces global semantics for the random lambda calculus. The increasing availability of massive electronic health records has fueled interest in utilizing vast medical datasets for building prediction models. While current approaches often rely on embedding layers for representations and attention mechanisms for feature selection to optimize performance on specific tasks, these issues limit interpretability, obscuring the specific contributions of individual embeddings to final outcomes. This study investigates a cohesive perspective for deep relational learning to enhance the transparency of medication-interaction predictions. Specifically, we introduce an artificial pipeline that captures semantic information from medications to medication pairs and calculates scores for these interactions. Our model demonstrates strong correlation between its calculated scores and existing databases of drug-drug mechanisms, outperforming or matching top-peroring models in current literature for predicting drug pair classifications.

Identifying road hazards such as potholes is crucial for ensuring public safety and maintaining infrastructure. While numerous automated detection systems have been developed, the majority rely on data collected by smartphones, which often results in poor detection rates caused by unsteady phone recordings. Furthermore, because these systems are trained for specific countries, they lack the ability to detect hazards in other regions due to differences in road environments and hazard characteristics. This study introduces two key contributions: a novel methodological approach to enhance the low quality of phone footage, and a new dataset named MultiNation containing footage from four distinct nations to facilitate more robust model training. In addition, we propose a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture for efficient hazard detection in auto-driving contexts. Finally, to further address performance limitations in low-resolution video, we introduce a novel image upscaling technique tailored for video super-resolution tasks.

Imitation distribution shift arises when a model trained on a training set $\mathbf{A}$ attempts to imitate a target expert $\pi^*$ in the test environment, resulting in a discrepancy between the two contexts. Although prior research addressed the general solution for such problems in settings where access to $\pi^*$ is direct, this paper focuses specifically on scenarios where the expert is observable only through past trajectories within the target environment. Under the assumption that $\pi$ and the target environment share a Markov structure, we develop a near-optimal approach. Our findings include rigorous upper and lower bounds for distribution shift metrics under both known and unknown environment transition dynamics, demonstrating that cross-area generalization performance is governed by the maximum information gap concerning the target environment. Additionally, we provide a cross-area improvement by directly addressing the resulting distribution shift through iterative refinement, thereby enhancing ICM performance.

A significant challenge in the early Universe involves forming the first massive Population III (Pop III) stars, which requires growing protostars to extreme masses ($\gtrsim 100\,M_\odot$) despite the disruptive influence of vertical gravity from the hosting galaxy's disk. We propose that strong, vertically enhanced magnetic fields generated by Pop III protostars can counteract disk fragmentation, thereby preventing star formation near the center and enabling the accumulation of mass onto the growing star instead. Our findings indicate that the disk-fragmentation-driven growth phase can be bypassed entirely if the disk's vertical-to-vertical differential rotation combined with the magnetorotational instability (MRI) amplifies magnetic fields by a factor exceeding $10^3$. Alternatively, a similar amplification could result from the interaction between the protostellar star and disk, creating a current sheet that amplifies fields via magnetic reconnection dynamics within this system. These results demonstrate that vertically intensified magnetic fields offer a viable mechanism for massive Pop III star formation at early cosmic times, complementing existing theories regarding accretion flows.

Association rules are a standard method for describing associations among variables, and their interpretation relies on a dedicated deducial framework. This paper defines the rule's logical structure using a repetition deduction framework (RDF), an approach that characterizes association rules as the most concise information they convey beyond the occurrences in a given dataset (or boolean expression). Consequently, finding the smallest possible rule base (MRBF) under an RDF constitutes a variation of an RDF-based interpretation. This study analyzes the MRBF problem within both traditional and complementary contexts. Traditional contexts assume the absence of dual relationships (like AND/OR) and seek the shortest linear sequence of associations, whereas complementary contexts explicitly model these relationships to find the shortest tree-shaped deducial framework. We present upper and lower bounds for MRBF in linearity and tree structures, respectively, and offer a polynomial-time algorithm to find the shortest tree. Finally, we provide the inaugural results linking tree-based MRBF to linear sequences under an RDF, establishing a bijective correspondence between the two structures while explaining specific properties of linear sequences through this lens.

This paper investigates how mental illness influences criminal behavior and examines whether mandating mental health treatment within the criminal justice system can reduce recidism. Using data from the National Survey of Criminal Justice, which tracks offenders over time, the study finds strong evidence linking mental illness to criminal activity among individuals convicted of crimes. The results indicate that those exhibiting symptoms of mental illness have a significantly higher likelihood of reoffending compared to peers without such conditions, a trend that persists even after controlling for initial crime severity, the extent of treatment received, and the participants' educational backgrounds these results suggest offering mental healthcare within correctional frameworks could potentially curb future criminal acts. Those who are offered healthcare have lower recidism rates than comparable convicts denied such access, though further investigation is warranted to definitively ascertain causality.

Dynamically selecting frequencies is becoming increasingly vital for next-generation wireless networks, necessitating the creation of large-scale 3D radio maps across both time and space dimensions. To construct these maps, sensors must gather extensive signal strength data throughout space, a task traditionally hindered by the high costs and limited ranges associated with human operators and equipment. To overcome these limitations, this paper proposes leveraging autonomous drones as a solution for aerial spectrum exploration. The core innovation lies in equipping the drones with Software-Defined Radios (SDR) and Machine Learning (ML) capabilities to autonomously identify and follow specific signal sources without direct human guidance. Furthermore, to enhance detection efficiency, the drones utilize software to adjust their flight altitude based on the Doppler effect and the Doppler Ramp. Initial validation of this framework was conducted in a controlled 3D environment using a simulated SDR drone and an ML-driven autonomous agent, successfully demonstrating the method's real-world viability.

Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) are a statistical modeling class that infer hidden states from observation sequences, finding extensive use in time-series analysis. While prior research has attempted to leverage HMMs for anomaly detection, no study has specifically addressed the issue of identifying anomalies in multivariate time-series data composed of numerous independent variables, such as those from industrial sensor arrays, by utilizing the model's conditional probability evaluations. In this paper, we propose an HMM-based anomaly detection framework that utilizes gauge probability evaluations to assess deviations from normal joint distributions across all variables simultaneously. This approach ensures robust detection even with sparse data or highly dependent sequences by relying on a unified model that captures underlying data generation mechanisms. We validate the efficacy of our method through experiments on both artificial datasets and real-world industrial power consumption logs.

However, this expansion is constrained by language barriers, as resources like labeled data and computational power are scarce in many languages. We assessed its efficacy across ASR and MT tasks in five languages, comparing our method against leading augmentative strategies like back-translation, synthetic text generation, and audio synthesis. Assessments utilized evaluation metrics from both as well as development sets representing monolingual languages. This study introduces a generalized maximum likelihood approach designed to estimate the mean of a mixture distribution defined by unknown weights and distinct component parameters, assuming available estimators for each part. The methodology accounts for scenarios involving overlapping parameter estimation with constraints, such as non-negativity, and is illustrated through a sampling application. In this context, it calculates the average time or duration of various tasks across three operational states: idle, busy, and service.

Standard differential privacy safeguards sensitive attributes within a dataset against an unbounded adversary with unlimited statistical capabilities. In practice, however, this model assumes no prior knowledge about the data, a restrictive premise that excludes knowledge about the data's dependency characteristics. To address this reality, we enhance standard differential privacy by accounting for the correlation between features. Specifically, we establish bounds on the information leakage regarding the target variable when the adversary already knows how that variable depends on the non-sensitive data. Our approach, grounded in the framework of one-sided differential privacy, is particularly suited for contexts like genomic research, where binary dependency knowledge effectively reveals sensitive information even in one-directional queries.

A significant outer gap in AS 209's CO spectrum is a defining characteristic. While previous research posited solid planet formation as the mechanism causing this feature, our study offers an alternative explanation: CO depletion driven by chemical activity. We assessed this hypothesis using two chemical models, one constrained by UV flux and lacking it, which tested variations in CO depletion percentage and accretion rates to match observed maps. The findings indicate that initial CO depletion at 30 AU is unattainable through chemistry within 2 Myr regardless of whether UV radiation is accounted for, unless accretion exceeds 0.01 Msun/yr by over an order of magnitude. However, our results suggest a much lower rate (around 0.002 +/- 0.001 Msun/yr) for the system. Instead, we propose a multi-component structure for the seen ring: an inner ring (15-30 AU) shaped by planetesimal formation and an outer ring (40-60 AU) formed through chemical processing.

The examination of time-stamped data is fundamental across numerous scientific domains, yet the availability of accessible, well-tested software tools supporting such analysis remains limited. To address this gap, we have developed a comprehensive suite of applications designed for the rigorous analysis of coincident time-stamped information. These tools are particularly crucial in modern spectroscopy for investigating the dynamics of electronic and structural transitions. Relying on the widely distributed professional spectrum analyzer, these applications allow users to generate time-stamped datasets from various sources and further enable the stacking of multiple traces for post-acquisition filtering. Specifically, the zero-correlation threshold can subsequently be imposed. Additionally, the capacity to correlate pairs or multiples of traces is explored, allowing correlated time-stamped data to coincide. Contrarily, uncorrelated signals can effectively be eliminated via these measures. This software runs on standard computer hardware and is written entirely in the language known to most users of the spectrum analyzer, enabling the easy creation of new tools and the straightforward integration with existing systems.

In this paper, we establish the presence of so-called "MILD" (strongly continuous semigroups associated with non-local terms and control constraints) solutions to specific restricted state-control mean field games under the influence of controls. Building upon the foundational work by Acemoglu et al. (2009), we further demonstrate the uniqueness of these solutions when the Hamiltonian is linear. De parting from traditional assumptions, our approach specifically addresses the absence of classic monotonicity conditions typically found in Hamiltonians—particularly those involving non-local components—and incorporates the noted state-control restrictions. Crucially, our method employs a "Free Boundary" formulation to mitigate the challenges posed by these non-local operators within a linear framework.

Recent high-resolution surveys, such as Gaia DR3, have identified extensive chains of stars within the Galaxy that were previously overlooked, prompting proposals to use these features for a more precise determination of the Milky Way's structure and dynamics. However, we argue that many such "threads" were previously unrecognized due to limited resolution and that a significant number of them result from the line-of-sight superposition of distinct stellar populations. By utilizing the VVV-III survey data to construct three-dimensional maps along the Galactic plane, we demonstrate that many apparent threads are merely visual artifacts caused by these superposed structures. We further investigate the extent to which stellar threads can reliably inform our understanding of the Galaxy's properties and their historical evolution.

Discrepancy detection in visual products is a visual query task that has garnered significant interest from various stakeholders, including e-commerce operators, marketers, and various users. In real-world scenarios, identifying visual inconsistencies between similar items, such as apparel, offers practical advantages like enhancing user shopping experiences, improving organic search relevance, and enriching product listings. Although visual attribute recognition has been extensively explored, leveraging these capabilities to address the visual discrepancy task has received limited attention. To address this, we introduce VICTOR, a novel approach that utilizes fashion-domain-specific contrastive pre-training alongside a discrepancy module designed to pinpoint variations between garments. VICTOR achieves superior performance on the public fashion discrepancy benchmark compared to other methods, marking a significant advancement in applying general visual attribute recognition to specific product inconsistency tasks.

This research paper presents a comprehensive examination of the spectrum of nonclassicality within quantum illumination, focusing on how entangled light enhances detection sensitivity beyond classical limits. We analyze how various states—ranging from single-photon Fock states to coherent superpositions of Fock states, as well as squeezed and anti-squeezed states like SLS (two-mode squeezed vacuum)—transcend traditional boundaries. Furthermore, we survey the development of nonclassicality metrics applicable across diverse illumination scenarios and discuss how robust quantum advantages remain valid despite noise and loss. As quantum illumination evolves, these resources continue to drive further breakthroughs in quantum sensing and imaging technologies.

Non-convex optimization within federated learning (FL) environments remains challenging due to its dependence on initial conditions and susceptibility to getting stuck in suboptimal local solutions. Standard approaches often mitigate this by increasing the number of gradient steps per communication round, yet such methods risk amplifying optimization noise. This paper introduces BAGA, a communication-efficient asynchronous aggregation algorithm designed to recover an unconstrained optimal path. By allowing the server to accumulate gradients from multiple clients across several rounds before performing updates, BETA leverages this accumulation phase to drive the optimization deeper into the trajectory, thereby reducing the count of frequent communication interactions required. Under the assumption of asynchrony, we provide an analysis of how this unconstrained trajectory influences convergence rates for generic stochastic smooth optimization with unimodal noise, specifically establishing that the expected decrease in objective function values correlates with both the local curvature at stationary points and the variance of gradient estimation. We further prove that, for smooth stochastic optimization with noise governed by a multiplicative structure, BAGA achieves a rate of $O\left(\frac{\log^{3/2}(L)}{ \sqrt{C}} + \frac{\sqrt{L}}{C} \right)$ for reaching an $\varepsilon$-stationary point, where $L$ denotes the accumulated gradient steps and $C$ stands for the system's communication rounds. Empirical results confirm BETA's efficacy in real-world scenarios.

It is argued that a dark matter component Primed Black Holes (PBHs) is viable under certain conditions derived from these frameworks. Specifically, by invoking the Shadow Dimension decompilation mechanism, we demonstrate compliance with various shapland conjectures, allowing for a negative cosmological constant in five-dimensional AdS geometry while maintaining a four-dimensional (4D) Minkowski or de Sitter effective landscape. The mechanics of layered systems, including biological tissues and geological strata, are heavily influenced by interfaces between layers. While previous research has mainly examined scenarios with perfectly adhered, defect-free interfaces, real-world systems often exhibit localized weak spots that lower the energy required to break adherence. This investigation explores how crack-like defects at interfaces give rise to cracks within one of the substrates. Our findings reveal that the pattern of internal cracking is governed by the specific location of the weak zone and the mechanical properties of both layers. Additionally, we outline the conditions necessary for self-healing.

The identification of substrate systems that facilitate both the formation of GaN monolayer epitaxy and high-quality electronic transport is essential for scalable Gallium Nitride devices. In this study, we employ first-principles calculations to explore the lattice matching between GaN and the wurtzite phases of MgSiN$_2$ and ZnGeN$_2$. Our results reveal that aligning a GaN layer along the [10$\overline{1}$0] direction onto a [000$\overline{1}$] orientation of these substrates induces a specific anisotropic in-plane strain. Notably, this strain engineering boosts the valence band hole mobility by as much as a factor of three compared to unstrained growth on a sapphire substrate.

This study addresses navigation challenges for underwater robots, such as AUVs and USVs, which must operate in unpredictable environments characterized by chaotic magnetic and gravitational fields, as well as highly non-linear sea bottom topography. Since online map creation and path planning are often hindered by these environmental complexities, the proposed solution introduces a Sparse Gaussian Process (SGP) model specifically for capturing temporal changes in the seafloor maps. By employing SGPs to represent time dynamics and utilizing a Kernels with an explicit structure for calculating the Natural Parameters (NP) through the marginal likelihood, the method achieves computational efficiency. This approach reduces data sparsity compared to traditional Gaussian Processes, allowing for faster inference. The new SG-Kernels are validated through simulations, and the method's efficacy is further demonstrated by successfully generating real-time paths for an Underwater Unmanned Surface Vehicle (USV) navigating a simulated aquatic terrain.

This study extends previous research by B. Y. Chen concerning surfaces in $\mathbb{R}^3$ equipped with meromorphically isotropic conformal parametrizations. Specifically, we generalize a result from B.Y.Chen to introduce and analyze properties of Calapso and Darboux functions defined within meromorphically isotropic surfaces. Furthermore, we generalize a theorem by B.Y.Chen regarding the commutativity of these transformations for such surfaces, establishing that in this context both the Calapso and Darboux transformations commute with one another.

This study presents contributions to local polynomial smoothing, specifically addressing the conditional mean regression problem. Adopting a nonparametric approach, the authors develop novel estimators that achieve first-order efficiency regardless of the conditional variance structure of the response variable.

Identities concerning the $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind have attracted significant attention over the past two decades. Link prediction represents a key application of knowledge graphs (KGs), where existing models typically integrate both vector-based static methods and recurrent dynamic approaches to evolve entity-relational states over time. We introduce a novel strategy that integrates temporal embeddings of entities and relations with temporal interval signals, subsequently passing this integrated information through a time-diffusion encoder to generate final KG representations. Demonstrated results confirm that this lightweight method rivals the performance of complex dynamic alternatives on both single and multi-relational KG datasets.

Although recent methods for detecting communities have a solid theoretical basis, the widely used hypergraph models they rely on are often poorly aligned with the actual goal of community detection when constructed from data. Clinical high-quality radiographs demand precise image-to-image annotations to facilitate the development of advanced radiological reading aids. Microcavity lasers are widely regarded as a prime source for generating nonclassical light, a capability essential for advancing quantum technologies. We reverse a many-body problem concerning random growth in surfaces by connecting the entries of a random matrix to those of a scattering matrix. During the March 28, 2016, fly-through by the Magnetospheric Multiscale (MMS) mission through the solar wind, two distinct events were recorded featuring electron-scale compressions that exhibited turbulence characteristics. The typical thickness of these compressions was approximately 100 $d_i$ (ion gyroradii), while their internal structures were organized into packet trains with average durations of around 2.2 $g_i^{-1}$ (the ion gyroperiod). Furthermore, the study suggests a relationship where shorter, highly nonlinear compressive packets with the steepest spectral slopes likely contribute most significantly to the energy cascade at electron scales.

This paper addresses a novel scenario by introducing hypergraphs to represent population contacts and adapting an approach originally developed by Callaway et al. [1]—which uses an uninfected recovery threshold—to this new structure. By extending the method to incorporate effective recovery numbers within hypergraph frameworks, we derive bounds for the extinction of an epidemic, accounting for the intricate, multi-way interactions these graphs capture. Our findings significantly generalize the results presented in [1], and numerical investigations suggest that our new bounds offer greater precision.

The recent discovery of magnetic semiconducting CrI₃, a material characterized by antiferromagnetic coupling between layers within its exchange interaction, has attracted significant attention. This interest stems from the potential to control magnetism in 2D ferromagnetic states via an out-of-plane magnetic field, enabling chiral magnetism at the interface. This study provides a theoretical analysis of spin textures in a basic square-lattice 2D ferroantimagnet like CrI₃. We identify that a byproduct of the Rashba effect is a distinctive spiral spin configuration, where the spin precession axis remains fixed, while precessing planes for adjacent layers are perpendicular. Notably, the presence of this interlayer orthogonality defines a chirality that can be toggled externally via a perpendicular magnetic field. This effect is most prominent when exchange interactions are antiferromagnetic between layers. We further demonstrate that non-zero spin chirality induces characteristic Hall signals—including anomalous Hall effect, spin Hall effect, and off-diagonal magnetization—and offers robust protection for magnetic skyrmions through balanced exchange terms. These findings establish solid theoretical groundwork for exploring chiral magnetic dynamics in future magnetic spintronic applications based on van der Waals ferromagnets.

Differential rotation, a defining trait of main-sequence stars, drives magnetic field generation. In solar-type stars, this differential spin is typically latitudinally sheared with high intensity at mid-latitudes but fades near the poles and equator. Conversely, as stellar age advances, convection zones expand, pushing low-activity latitudinal bands inward, thereby increasing dynamo influence on nearer equatorial regions where rotation becomes increasingly sluggish. This dynamical shift raises the critical inquiry: can stars sustain magnetic cycles despite the anti-solar nature of their differential rotation? Addressing this, we utilized the magnetic core-sun (MCD) framework to simulate both ad-solar (Sun) and anti-solar (young) differential rotations across a range of rotation amplitudes. Our results indicate that stars exhibiting anti-solar rotation patterns can indeed sustain magnetic cycles, provided the rotation remains sufficiently vigorous. Furthermore, while the root-mean-square total magnetic field strength remains comparable between the solar-type (satisfying) and young systems, the average helicity diverges significantly. We conclude that slow-rotating regions, such as those observed in youthful stars, possess the capacity for cyclical magnetic behavior, though the underlying small-scale magnetic architecture and helicity remain distinct from the Sun.

To address multimodal classification tasks, this paper introduces UKFD-FAN, an innovative universal deep framework designed to handle diverse input configurations such as modual sets, single modes, or even isolated data points. The architecture utilizes a hierarchical arrangement of dense layers supplemented by specific substructures: an adaptation layer to manage varying dimensions, a normalization (K-norm) and flipping (flip-ing) process known as "K-fan," and a representation learning component ensuring efficient knowledge transfer across modes. Curated training using curated datasets enhances performance, while the framework's superior flexibility enables robust training even with uncurated or non-standardizing unlabeled data. Comprehensive evaluations across fourteen datasets demonstrate that UKFD-FAN achieves state-of-the-art results in classification accuracy and significantly reduces training time compared to existing leading models.

Model verification utilizing time-schedule pairs has proven to be an effective method for detecting bugs in multi-threaded programs, yet existing solutions typically suffer from either excessive false positives or prohibitive computational costs. To address these issues, we introduce McMini, a new verifier that builds upon Data-Race Detection with Priority Reordering (DPOR). McMini achieves two key objectives: the elimination of phantom failures and a substantial reduction in computational complexity. Its efficiency stems from leveraging Mini, a minimalist static analyzer, to conduct conditional pre-detection of data races. This mechanism drastically minimizes the set of schedules requiring detailed dynamic analysis. Furthermore, we describe enhancements that dynamically adapt detailed analysis based on the specific program context. McMini was evaluated on two open-source projects and a closed-source product containing thousands of lines of code, demonstrating superior performance over current state-of-the-art tools, particularly in cases involving extensive data structures.

The proliferation of fake news, coupled with the lack of effective tools to manage its distribution, remains a pressing issue. Researchers have observed that social media platforms, including major ones, are primary vectors for disseminating misinformation, often due to features like unlimited message forwarding. Specifically, WhatsApp has restricted this feature, initially allowing messages to be forwarded only once, later increasing the cap to five instances. Given that the average share count on such platforms often exceeds the permitted limit in WhatsApp, the platform imposed a daily limit instead. This study investigates the impact of these forwarding restrictions on the propagation of mis- and disinformation within the network. The findings suggest that standard linear and message-specific limitations do not necessarily curb the spread of false information. However, implementing a new approach that monitors contextual cues and limits the number of recipients per unique message demonstrates significant efficacy. Surprisingly, a proposed limit culling messages deemed "suspicious" and capping total shares at ten is more potent than reducing the limit to the platform's current policy of ten total messages per user. Real-world data analysis of over 1,000 news articles and their associated sharing behaviors in English-speaking contexts (specifically the U.K. and U.S.) supports these results.

We introduce a method to estimate the infinite-sites branching allelic frequency spectrum (BAFS) $\phi(u)$, which describes the distribution of mutant allele frequencies resulting from a single mutation event in a general supercritical branching process with known parameters. This spectrum is a normalized, time-independent measure representing the proportion of lineages carrying a mutation that has relative frequency $v$ at time $t > 0$. We first establish that the BAFS exists and derive formulas to compute it via Laplace transforms of our proposed estimator, which converge almost surely within a broad setting. We subsequently evaluate the bias of this estimator by simulating evolutionary events over fixed time intervals containing a known number of mutations; the simulation results confirm that the estimator performs accurately for various population models, including critical branching with linear growth, subcritical branching with $1-\alpha$ Bessel process population sizes, and supercritical branching with linear growth.

Speech activation functions (SAFs) are a fundamental component of spoofing countermeasure pipelines, serving to filter out genuine audio inputs to avoid false security breaches. However, existing functions fail to maintain an optimal balance between two critical factors: minimizing the false rejection rate (FRR) and ensuring low latency. This tension is particularly acute in systems utilizing deep neural networks (DNNs), where there has been a historical reliance on the hard sigmoid function. This choice often induces excessive DNN latency, causing the overall activation stage latency to exceed the strict time constraints required for effective audio protection. This study introduces novel parametric functions capable of regulating DNN latency to match predefined thresholds, simultaneously optimizing FRR performance.

Einstein-Grojanik-Rosen (EGR) inflation models, which exhibit the AdS/dS CFT correspondence, are of particular interest. This study presents a novel approach to deriving locally supersymmetric effective field theories (EFTs) for local brane setups, specifically targeting the EGR-type scenarios. We establish a duality between EGR-type models and BPS egg configurations, allowing us to construct the EGR-supersymmetry by analyzing the supersymmetry of the egg system. Furthermore, we identify a set of BPS egg-derived supersymmetry algebras that may yield efficient, locally supersymmetric EGTs, with one variant, the ESR-type EGR model, noted for the first time to possess local supersymmetry.

Photonic four-wave mixing in $\chi^{(3)}$ media generates entangled photon pairings, yet the intensity-resolved spatial correlation (ICSC) functions for these pairs often display symmetry. This study introduces theoretically predicted asymmetric PHSPs and experimental verification, contrasting sharply with the typical symmetric properties of entangled photon pair spatial correlations. The observed asymmetric PHSPs arise specifically from the interchangeability of up and down converted photons within the symmetric Fock state $|n,n\rangle$. Crucially, these asymmetries in PHSPs enable the determination of the sign for $n$ in $|n,n\rangle$, a task previously unachievable through two-photon coincidence counts alone, while maintaining robustness against noise.

This work examines the electromagnetic fields of microwave-resonator cavities using both numerical methods and near-field optical microscopy. The numerical analysis is grounded in the principle that the electromagnetic modes of a resonator, whether it features sharp or rounded corners, can be constructed by superposing the mode patterns of an ideal rectangular cavity without such irregularities. Consequently, any structural deviation from a rectangle generates energy localization within regions of known field maxima of these component fundamental modes. Optical microscopy results were obtained at wavelengths around 0.1 micrometers, significantly smaller than the resonator's dimensions (on the order of 10 micrometers). As energy localization occurs over length scales much larger than the probe resolution (micrometer scale), the far-field energy distribution was observed instead. Numerical predictions align closely with the experimental data. Consequently, the study demonstrates that resonator geometry profoundly influences the spatial localization of microwave modes and dictates the structure of their in-plane distributions.

Let $\mathcal{R}$ represent the real line, $\mathfrak{c}$ the cardinality of the continuum, and $(R_{\alpha})_{\alpha < \omega_1}$ an enumeration of $\mathbb R$. This work presents a method to partition $\mathbb R$ into $\omega_1$ Borel sets $\{C_\alpha : \alpha < \omega_1\}$ such that for every pair of countable ordinals $\beta, \gamma$, the cardinality of their intersection is either $0$ or $\ 1$. Specifically, there exists such a partition where each set $C_\alpha$ intersects $R_{\alpha}$, ensuring non-emptiness. Given any assignment of cardinalities $\{M_\alpha : \alpha < \omega_1\}$ to these components such that each $M_\alpha$ is either empty or has cardinal $\mathfrak c$, there exists an extension of the partition $\{C_\alpha : \alpha < \omega_1\}$ such that each $(C_\alpha \cap R_{\alpha}) \subseteq M_\alpha$. These constructions rely on a combinatorial result concerning the hypergraph theory of finite subsets of $\mathbb N$.

Financial markets are constantly shifting; consequently, agents must adapt their tactics to secure higher returns. This study examines how strategies perform in changing environments using an model where agents employ techniques derived from literature alongside those newly invented on the fly to bid for assets. We investigate how the presence of these innovative methods impacts current investments' performance. Results show that agents must adjust their tactics in response to those new ones to maintain high performance and mitigate risk. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this continuous introduction of innovations drives the cumulative returns of current holdings more than does environmental variation alone.

The author presents a novel attack method targeting the protocol identification mechanisms of dynamic analysis tools, extending previous techniques [1] to target the widely-used Snort intrusion detection system. Although initially effective in specific, narrowly defined network conditions, these original methods proved difficult to deploy reliably in general scenarios. In contrast, this study introduces a more versatile attack strategy designed with greater practical deployability in mind. Beyond expanding on the limitations of the prior art, the work also outlines several optimizations and improvements to further bolster the success rate of these traditional breaks. Ultimately, the paper emphasizes the critical necessity of robust protocol identification, particularly for systems relying on dynamic analysis, by illustrating the severe consequences that can result from successful compromises.

Placing materials that naturally reject magnetic fields next to magnetic sources can generate boundaries where magnons (collective spin excitations) are perfectly excluded, similar to how quantum waves flow around obstacles in superconductors. This study reports the first observation of magnons navigating a series of such barriers and tunnels through them in an exchange-bias bilayer made of yttrium iron oxide and nickel. By controlling the degree of superconducting properties induced in the nickel, researchers can adjust both the height and width of these magnonic barriers. The findings confirm that superconducting regions act as effective potential walls for magnons, offering new methodologies to structure magnonic devices at micro and nano scales using superconductors.

Distributed learning networks for audio classification often face bandwidth constraints, necessitating that most computations occur on the client side while transmitting only limited parameters to the server. Concurrently, the rapid evolution of data categorization schemes makes it costly and cumbersome to retrain existing models from scratch whenever new classification schemes emerge. In this paper, we introduce a novel zero-shot learning approach that enables both novel class data ingestion and model adaptation with minimal server-client communication. This method begins by training a global model on a large, unlabeled dataset covering extensive classes, which is then partitioned and deployed to all clients. Upon local fine-tuning with task-specific new class data, each client transmits both their localized global model parameters and localized data to the server for aggregation. Finally, the resulting global model is distributed again to all clients. We evaluate this approach on the DCASE 2020 Task 3 dataset and compare it against current baselines. Empirical results indicate that this zero-shot learning algorithm enhances detection performance in challenging real-world acoustic environments.
